say: Today the fictional hotel coordinator needs to communicate the work, not just manage or document it. We'll build a customer story, respond to changed requirements, and turn a training workbook into a board-level discussion.

The useful outcome isn't a deck that happens to look finished. It's a presentation whose audience, messages, and evidence fit together, with open decisions still visible and a person checking the story before it is shared.
welcome.ask: What makes a presentation trustworthy beyond having polished slides?
welcome.watch: Frame the workshop around source-based storytelling; don't imply the illustrated decks are approved outputs.

say: The coordinator has three requests with different audiences and evidence: shape a customer presentation from a Word source, rebuild when a revision arrives, and tell the board what the workbook supports. A slide that works for one request may be wrong for another.

Before creating anything, identify which source controls the facts for that task. The outdated deck can help us compare, but it can't override a newer requirement simply because its slide already looks convincing.
request.ask: Which source should control the rebuilt customer story, and which should control the board charts?
request.watch: Point to the three requests; distinguish customer reassurance from board decision-making.

say: Follow the route from gathering evidence and shaping a story to building, refreshing, visualising, and reviewing. We're not beginning with a slide layout because we first need to know what the audience should understand or decide.

The same discipline applies when the facts change: revisit the controlling source, reshape the message, then verify the output. Faster slide generation doesn't help if superseded details survive in a persuasive-looking presentation.
flow.ask: Which move prevents us from building a polished deck around the wrong story?
flow.watch: Trace the six moves; connect refresh to rechecking sources rather than merely changing visual styling.

say: Check your access to the work chat route, PowerPoint, and the four training files before we start. We'll be moving between analysing sources in chat and building presentations, so knowing which environment you're in will save confusion later.

If you can't use the PowerPoint exercise on your device, follow my demonstration and still take part in the evidence checks. The reasoning about sources, audiences, and unsupported claims doesn't depend on everyone generating an identical deck.
needs.ask: Can you follow both the chat and PowerPoint parts, or do you need the demonstration for one of them?
needs.watch: Check actual access; identify demo-following learners without promising a capability their environment doesn't show.

say: Download the four practice sources and notice that they aren't all the same file type. We have the presentation source in Word, a revised PDF pack, a performance workbook, and an outdated PowerPoint deck.

Keep those originals unchanged so we can compare them throughout the workshop. Their different roles are intentional, and the fictional event and numbers let us practise difficult source decisions without using real customer material.
get.ask: Can you identify all four files and the type of evidence each will provide?
get.watch: Confirm the complete source pack; keep the old deck separate from presentations learners create today.

say: Create the Tell the Story folder in your work OneDrive and place the four sources there for the selection route shown in this lesson. We'll also keep the suggestions, comparison, and new decks together as the exercise develops.

Check the actual contents before leaving setup rather than assuming the download completed the preparation. Clear names and one working location will help us select the right version when the revision arrives and when we run the final verification.
folder.ask: Can you see the four originals in Tell the Story without confusing them with a new output?
folder.watch: Verify uploads and filenames; frame this as the workshop route rather than a universal file-access restriction.

say: Read the source roles before asking for a presentation: the Word document starts the customer story, the revised PDF controls later changes, and the workbook controls numerical claims. The old deck is material for comparison, not the authority for the updated event.
When documents disagree, don't silently blend them into a compromise. Identify the conflict and use the controlling source, while keeping anything it doesn't settle visible as an open item.
files.ask: Why would averaging or blending conflicting old and revised event details be the wrong approach?
files.watch: Point to the source hierarchy; test one conflict verbally without introducing facts outside the pack.

say: Scan the Word presentation source yourself before asking Copilot to recommend a story. Notice the customer audience, the event purpose, the guest journey, and the decisions the file still leaves open.

You don't need to memorise every detail, but you should be able to recognise when the answer changes the sequence or fills a gap. That initial reading gives you something concrete to compare with the recommendations we'll generate next.
read.ask: What is one confirmed part of the guest journey and one decision the customer still needs to make?
read.watch: Allow silent source reading; ask for evidence rather than answers remembered from the illustrative slides.

say: Write a short answer for audience, purpose, confirmed facts, open items, and the story you want the presentation to tell. This is your thinking space before you ask Copilot to structure the material.

Keep the customer in mind rather than listing everything the hotel knows internally. A useful storyline connects what matters to that audience, while an open item remains something to discuss rather than an assumption that makes the slide feel complete.
canvas.ask: What should the customer understand or decide after seeing your presentation?
canvas.watch: Give learners time to write the five answers in their own note; don't imply the page stores them.

say: Use Prompt 1 with the Word source to gather the audience, purpose, confirmed facts, open items, guest journey, and suggested story. We're asking for the ingredients and a structure before opening a presentation.

Compare the recommendation with the canvas you just wrote rather than giving up your own view of the audience. The answer should help organise the evidence, not invent details to make the event sound more reassuring.
t1do.ask: Which part of your own story canvas will you compare most carefully with Copilot's recommendation?
t1do.watch: Select file 1 in the work chat route; wait for the actual response before discussing its accuracy.

say: Check your real recommendation using the questions beside the illustrated example. Confirm that it speaks to the customer, keeps open items separate, and preserves the source's guest-journey sequence.

A confident story can be misleading if an unresolved approver, quantity, or decision disappears from view. Trace the important statements back to the Word document, and keep the suggested storyline as a recommendation rather than treating it as new evidence.
t1ok.ask: Which open item is easiest to lose when your recommendation becomes a short customer story?
t1ok.watch: Inspect the learner's response, not the example's six sections; check one journey detail and one open item.

say: Save the checked recommendation as a Word output using the answer menu route demonstrated here, adapting to the controls your environment shows. Name the suggestions file clearly so it can be selected alongside the original source for the next prompt.

This output helps carry the proposed storyline into PowerPoint, but it doesn't replace the original event evidence. Before leaving chat, check that the saved file contains the recommendation you reviewed rather than an earlier unchecked answer.
export.ask: How will you recognise the checked suggestions file when selecting sources for the first deck?
export.watch: Check the exported content and filename; don't assume the mock menu proves the learner's file was saved.

say: We've gathered the story ingredients, thought about the customer, and retained a checked recommendation for the next stage. That gives us a more purposeful starting point than asking for slides from an unfamiliar file.

Pause to make sure both the original Word source and your suggestions output are available. The first remains the evidence, while the second helps shape the story; keeping those roles distinct is important when we build.
cp1.ask: Which file provides the confirmed facts, and which provides the storyline suggestions?
cp1.watch: Check both Word files are available before you start Prompt 2.

say: Open a new presentation and use Prompt 2 with the original Word source and your saved suggestions file. Ask for message-led titles and a concise customer story covering purpose, guest journey, support, readiness, open decisions, and next steps.

Keep the source boundaries in the prompt so a proposed visual doesn't imply an unconfirmed service or facility. This gives us a first deck to inspect, not a promise that every generated slide will be accurate or suitable.
t2do.ask: What would make a slide title a useful message for the customer rather than just a topic label?
t2do.watch: Use the prompt as written with the two Word files; do not add real customer names.

say: Review the deck you actually generated for audience, storyline, evidence, density, visual meaning, and responsibility. The illustrated slide list helps explain the checks, but your deck may have a different structure.

Open a slide and trace its factual claims to the original source rather than the suggestions file alone. If you use optional Prompt 3, inspect its improvement list too; a second generated review doesn't remove your responsibility to check the presentation.
t2ok.ask: Which slide in your first deck needs the highest-priority improvement before it could be shared?
t2ok.watch: Review real slides rather than sample rows; treat Prompt 3 as optional and preserve time for mandatory final verification.

say: You now have a first customer deck and a clearer view of what it still needs. Keep that work available, but don't assume its facts will remain current when the event changes.
The next request introduces a revised source pack and an outdated deck for comparison. This pause marks the shift from building a story to deciding which details must be kept, changed, or removed.
cp2.ask: What would you recheck first if a revised event pack arrived after you had built your slides?
cp2.watch: Keep the first deck distinct from the supplied outdated deck; avoid mixing the two comparison inputs.

say: Read the late changes as changes to the story, not just replacements for a few numbers. Audience, timing, breakouts, catering, equipment, and updates can affect which messages the customer needs.

For each item, decide whether to keep, change, or remove it and state the source-based reason. The revised pack controls conflicts, but anything it still leaves unresolved must remain a question rather than a detail supplied to make the deck easier to finish.
changes.ask: Which revised requirement most changes the storyline rather than only a slide's wording?
changes.watch: Let learners inspect the revised pack; distinguish confirmed changes from still-open customer decisions.

say: Use a new chat with the revised PDF and the supplied outdated deck, then ask Prompt 4 for a keep, change, remove, and why table. This is the evidence bridge between the old presentation and the rebuilt story.

The prompt explicitly gives the revised pack control when details conflict. We still need to inspect the comparison, because a well-organised table can misread either source or hide an item that needs confirmation.
t4do.ask: What should the comparison say when the old deck and revised pack disagree about an event detail?
t4do.watch: Confirm files 2 and 4 are selected; don't accidentally compare the learner's first deck instead of the supplied old deck.

say: Check the rows in your own comparison against both files, including the old detail, the revised detail, and the reason for the change. Don't treat the tidy example table as a validated comparison.

The lesson highlights a lunch-description discrepancy between the pack's account of the earlier deck and the old deck itself. Use that as a reminder to open the files and report conflicts accurately, not as proof that your response necessarily contains the same error.
t4ok.ask: What does your comparison say about lunch, and have you checked both the old slide and the revised pack?
t4ok.watch: Inspect the actual lunch row against the sources; don't endorse the example's earlier-deck label without checking.

say: Save the checked comparison as a Word file so we can use it with the revised pack and outdated deck in the rebuilding task. Give it a clear changes-comparison name and check its contents after saving.

This file records your reviewed interpretation of the differences, not a replacement authority for the revised requirements. Carry forward any unresolved discrepancy explicitly so the next prompt doesn't turn it into a confident but unsupported slide detail.
export2.ask: What must you check in the saved comparison before attaching it to the rebuild prompt?
export2.watch: Verify the saved comparison reflects corrections; distinguish it from the earlier storyline suggestions file.

say: Start a new presentation for Prompt 5 rather than opening the outdated deck to patch it. Select the revised pack, the old deck for comparison, and your checked comparison file.

Ask for a new storyline that reflects the changed audience, programme, parallel breakouts, working lunch, equipment, update, risks, and decisions. Beginning again helps us inspect the story as a whole, but it still requires checking that superseded details haven't reappeared.
t5do.ask: Why might patching the old deck leave mistakes that are harder to notice than rebuilding the story?
t5do.watch: Confirm a new deck and the three intended sources; prevent editing the supplied old deck as the working output.

say: Review your rebuilt deck for one clear message per slide and trace the changed requirements to the revised pack. The sample storyline is a checking aid, not evidence that your generated deck contains the right details.

Look deliberately for leftovers from the old attendance, start time, or update wording, then check that risks and customer decisions remain visible. Removing old facts isn't enough if the presentation also hides what still needs to be agreed.
t5ok.ask: Which slide in your rebuilt deck is most likely to retain an old number or an unresolved decision?
t5ok.watch: Search actual slides for superseded details; don't claim the new storyline is clean until the learner checks it.

say: Save the rebuilt presentation as a clearly named PowerPoint file in the workshop folder, following the save route your environment shows. This is the new customer deck based on the revised requirements, not another copy of the outdated source.

Check that you can identify and reopen the new deck separately from the outdated source. We'll need that actual saved presentation for final verification, so naming and version clarity are part of preparing a reviewable output.
save7.ask: How will you identify the rebuilt deck, rather than the outdated source, during final verification?
save7.watch: Treat save7 as the Prompt 5 save step; verify the actual new PowerPoint file and location.

say: Use the revised pack's modern tropical evening direction to think about calm, readable visual treatment. The displayed palette and chart suggestions should support the message rather than distract from the customer decisions.

If you use optional Prompt 6, review its proposed imagery against the source boundaries before adopting it. An attractive venue image or icon can imply a facility or service the pack never confirmed, so visual choices need the same care as slide text.
style.ask: Which visual would clarify the revised event without implying an unconfirmed facility or service?
style.watch: Keep optional styling short; inspect readability and implied claims rather than treating appearance as verification.

say: The revised customer deck has been rebuilt, checked for the changed story, and saved as a separate output. Keep its unresolved items visible; finishing the rebuild doesn't mean every customer decision is settled.

We're about to change audiences and evidence again, this time to the board and the performance workbook. Pause here so the event revision doesn't get mixed with the numerical claims we'll make in the next presentation.
cp3.ask: What changes when we move from a customer event presentation to a board performance story?
cp3.watch: Keep the rebuilt customer deck retained; clearly signal the move to the workbook-based board task.

say: Read all three workbook sheets before asking for charts, including the monthly figures, event comparisons, and management notes. The highlighted September pattern is something to inspect in the fictional dataset, not a conclusion about a real hotel.
Look at labels and measures as well as the values, because the board story must say what is being compared. We need a source we understand before deciding which numbers deserve space on a slide.
data.ask: Which workbook sheet would you use to check a monthly trend, and which would explain event-type issues?
data.watch: Let the sheet transitions finish; have learners open the real training workbook and retain the fictional-data label.

say: Choose three to five measures because the board needs a focused discussion, not every column copied onto slides. For each choice, state what question it helps answer or what management action it might inform.

In this exercise, revenue must sit beside cost or margin so the financial story isn't reduced to income alone. Balance that with supported service or operational measures, and avoid selecting a number merely because it looks impressive.
metrics.ask: Which three to five measures would you choose, and what board question does each answer?
metrics.watch: Ask for reasons alongside selections; flag a revenue-only choice and trace measures to workbook labels.

say: Match the chart to the question: a monthly pattern, an event comparison, or the relationship between revenue, cost, and margin needs a different visual. Clear chart choices help the audience inspect the evidence rather than merely admire the slide.

The paired ratings and maintenance figures illustrate an important boundary: events happening together don't prove why they happened. Describe the observed pattern and leave causal explanations as questions unless the source supports them.
evidence.ask: How would you rewrite a claim that maintenance tickets caused lower ratings using only the observed workbook pattern?
evidence.watch: Compare the displayed causal and observational wording; avoid supplying a new explanation for the pattern.

say: Open a new board presentation and use Prompt 7 with the performance workbook. Ask for three to five supported measures, suitable charts, what appears to be going well, what needs attention, and the management question or action.

Keep the instructions to pair revenue with cost or margin and label the values as fictional training data. The story should distinguish what the workbook shows from explanations it cannot prove, even if a stronger causal claim would sound more dramatic.
t7do.ask: What caution should accompany a board slide that compares service ratings with maintenance activity?
t7do.watch: Select the workbook for the new deck; check the fictional label and evidence boundary remain in the copied prompt.

say: Check the board deck you actually received at three levels: the measures selected, the charts used, and the interpretation of the patterns. The illustrated charts aren't proof that your generated values or labels are correct.

Trace a plotted value back to its workbook cell and inspect whether the slide answers a real board question. Then look for a sentence that turns an observation into a cause or recommends an action without making its evidence boundary clear.
t7ok.ask: Which plotted value have you checked, and does the slide's conclusion stay within what the workbook supports?
t7ok.watch: Verify one chart value, its label, and the accompanying conclusion; don't assert the sample September story is the learner's output.

say: We've reached the final pause before verification, with the customer and board work available to review. There is one mandatory stage left, even if a deck already looks persuasive or a previous check found no obvious problems.

Make sure the presentation you want to verify is the current saved output and that its relevant sources are available. This checkpoint is readiness for the review task, not a declaration that the presentation itself is ready to share.
cp4.ask: Which current presentation and controlling sources will you bring into the final verification?
cp4.watch: Protect time for Prompt 8; confirm the selected deck version before starting the mandatory review.

say: Use Prompt 8 in a new chat with the presentation and the source files needed to verify it. Request checks of the audience, purpose, event details, numerical claims, decisions, owners, deadlines, and risks.

The answer should list unsupported or superseded content and end with a readiness recommendation plus required fixes. We're asking for a review of the actual output, so choosing the current deck and the correct controlling sources matters as much as copying the prompt.
t8do.ask: Which source should settle a conflict found in your deck during this final review?
t8do.watch: Check actual deck and source attachments; keep the mandatory verification separate from optional styling or first-draft review.

say: Read the verdict from your own verification response and inspect the evidence for each proposed fix. The example on screen is Not Ready, but that is not a prediction of your result or proof that those sample defects are present.

A Ready recommendation also needs scrutiny, especially if an open decision or unsupported claim was missed. Make the corrections you can justify, repeat the check where needed, and keep the final sharing decision with a person.
t8ok.ask: Which finding changes your decision about sharing the deck, and what source confirms that finding?
t8ok.watch: Don't announce the sample verdict as the learner's verdict; verify real findings and avoid treating Copilot as an approver.

say: We used different sources and audiences to shape a customer story, rebuild after changes, and present a focused view of fictional performance data. The connecting rule was to know which evidence controls each claim.

That rule applies to words, numbers, charts, and imagery, not just the final fact-check. A presentation becomes more useful when it explains what the audience needs, shows what is supported, and keeps decisions or uncertainty visible instead of smoothing them away.
recap.ask: Where did choosing the controlling source make the biggest difference to your presentation?
recap.watch: Recap the three tasks without guaranteeing trustworthy decks; connect each to a learner's actual verification.

say: Save the eight prompts so you can repeat the process of gathering, building, comparing, rebuilding, visualising, and verifying. The first-deck review and visual-treatment follow-up are optional, but the final verification is not optional in this workshop.

When you reuse a prompt, change the audience and select the right sources rather than carrying today's fictional details into another task. Keep the constraints that separate evidence from suggestions and prevent unsupported claims.
pack.ask: Which prompt would you use when a revised customer pack makes an existing presentation outdated?
pack.watch: Show the full pack download; distinguish optional Prompts 3 and 6 from mandatory Prompt 8.

say: You've practised shaping a story from evidence, rebuilding around revised requirements, selecting supported measures, and checking a presentation before use. The saved suggestions and comparison files helped carry your thinking between stages without replacing the sources.

For your next presentation, choose the audience and controlling evidence before asking for slides. Keep a clear version to review, trace important claims, and make the final decision yourself rather than letting visual polish or a generated verdict stand in for judgement.
learned.ask: What will you do differently before building your next presentation, and what will you verify before sharing it?
learned.watch: Close with one specific next habit; keep fictional training decks distinct from approved real-world presentations.
